name: Virginia City

stops.name: C Street
stops.teaser: The main street of a silver boom town.
stops.clue: Find the main street of Virginia City. Its name is just one letter. Two- and three-story brick buildings line it, and most of them went up after a huge fire in 1875.
stops.safety: Sidewalks are narrow and steep in places, and cars share the road. Cross only at corners. The town sits at about 6,100 feet, so bring water. Saloons and casinos are for adults, so stay out of them. None of the stops need you to go inside.
stops.field: Field notes pending: sidewalk surfaces and slopes have not been checked on foot yet.

q.prompt: Find the 'Great Fire of 1875' marker on the old hose house. What does it say started the fire?
q.hint: It started in a boarding house, on a morning in October.
q.verify: Nevada SHPO marker No. 228, near where the fire began. The street is not given. Confirm location and wording on site.

then.label: Virginia City from the hills
then.line: The archive dates this stereo photo somewhere between 1867 and 1920. About 25,000 people lived here in the mid-1870s, before the Great Fire.

link.t: Look for historic photos at the Library of Congress

now.head: Today
now.label: A National Historic Landmark
now.line: The whole historic district became a National Historic Landmark on July 4, 1961. Photo taken in 2015.

story: Silver was found here in 1859, and the Comstock Lode set off the first big silver rush. Virginia City was incorporated in February 1861.
By the mid-1870s more than 25,000 people lived here. On October 26, 1875, the Great Fire burned much of the town, did about $12 million in damage, and left about 2,000 people homeless.
The town was rebuilt. Most buildings along C Street are two- and three-story brick. Today about 800 people live here, at roughly 6,100 feet above sea level.
stops.fact: One year after the town was founded, it reportedly had 42 saloons, 42 stores, 6 restaurants, 3 hotels, and 868 homes.
stops.disputed: The story goes that the town was named when "Old Virginny" Finney broke a whiskey bottle at a saloon near Gold Hill. That is local folklore. The settlement also went by earlier names, such as Pleasant Hill and Mount Pleasant Point.

claims.t: The Great Fire of Virginia City happened on October 26, 1875.
claims.why: Sources agree on the date and on about $12 million in damage.

claims.t: Henry Comstock discovered the Comstock Lode.
claims.why: Peter O'Riley and Patrick McLaughlin are credited with the discovery. Comstock later attached his name to it and claimed a share.

spot.q: The old photo shows Virginia City before the Great Fire. What happened on October 26, 1875?
options: The fire burned much of the town and left about 2,000 people homeless
spot.why: The Great Fire did about $12 million in damage. The town was rebuilt, and most buildings along C Street are brick.

stops.name: Territorial Enterprise
stops.teaser: Where a young writer became Mark Twain.
stops.map: Mark Twain Museum, C Street, Virginia City, NV
stops.clue: Walk along C Street and look for the old newspaper building, now a museum with a famous writer's name on it.
stops.safety: Stay on the sidewalk. The museum is optional and has its own hours and rules. Look from the street.
stops.field: Field notes pending: the exact viewing spot has not been checked on foot yet.

q.prompt: Find the marker about Mark Twain. In what year does it say he first used that name?
q.hint: It is the year before he left the paper.
q.verify: Nevada Centennial Marker No. 28 (placed 1960). Its exact location was not found. Confirm on site.

then.label: The building in 1937
then.line: On February 3, 1863, a letter in this paper was signed "Mark Twain" for the first time. This photo of the building was taken in March 1937.

link.t: Look for historic photos at the Library of Congress

now.head: Today
now.label: Mark Twain Museum
now.line: A Mark Twain Museum operates in the original Territorial Enterprise building. Photo taken in 2010.

story: The Territorial Enterprise was founded on December 18, 1858, in Genoa, then part of Utah Territory. It moved to Carson City in 1859 and to Virginia City in 1860.

In 1862 a young writer named Sam Clemens began sending letters to the paper, and that fall he accepted a job as city editor. On February 3, 1863, he signed a funny letter about a party "Mark Twain" for the first time.
He worked at the paper until he left for San Francisco in 1864, alongside the writer Dan DeQuille. The two shared a room on North B Street, steps from the newspaper office.
stops.fact: The paper started in Genoa, Nevada, and moved twice before it landed in Virginia City.
stops.disputed: One list dates the newspaper building to 1862 and another to the 1870s. We could not find a record that settles it.

claims.t: Mark Twain first signed a letter with that name on February 3, 1863.
claims.why: Both the Mark Twain at the Territorial Enterprise page and History.com report that date.

claims.t: Twain lived inside the newspaper building.
claims.why: One source says he and Dan DeQuille shared a room on North B Street, steps from the office.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Mark Twain at the Territorial Enterprise
History.com: Mark Twain begins reporting in Virginia City

spot.q: The 1937 photo shows the Territorial Enterprise building. What did Sam Clemens first sign there on February 3, 1863?
options: A job contract in Carson City
spot.why: He signed a funny letter about a party "Mark Twain" for the first time. He worked at the paper until he left for San Francisco in 1864.

stops.name: Piper's Opera House
stops.teaser: A theater that burned down twice.
stops.map: Piper's Opera House, Virginia City, NV
stops.clue: Find the big theater at the corner of B Street and a cross street. Two earlier opera houses on the spot burned down. This is the third.
stops.safety: Stay on the sidewalk and cross at the corner. Hills here are steep, so watch your footing. Look at the building from outside.
stops.field: Field notes pending: curb cuts and the viewing spot have not been checked on foot yet.

q.prompt: Find the Nevada State Historic Marker at the opera house. What number is it?
q.hint: It is a three-digit number between 200 and 300.
q.verify: Marker 236 at 12 N. B Street per noehill.com. Confirm on site.

then.label: The third Piper's
then.line: It opened with a grand ball on March 6, 1885. This photo was taken in March 1937 for a historic buildings survey.

link.t: Look for historic photos at the Library of Congress

now.head: Today
now.label: A working theater
now.line: A nonprofit bought it in 1997, and it is a performing arts venue today. Photo taken in 2009.

story: John Piper's first opera house opened here in 1863. It burned in the Great Fire of October 26, 1875. A second one opened on January 28, 1878 and burned on March 13, 1883.
The building you see today opened with a grand ball on March 6, 1885. It switched from gas to electric lighting in 1900.

Mark Twain lectured on the original stage in 1866 and again in 1868. Later stars included Edwin Booth, Lillie Langtry, John Philip Sousa, and Al Jolson. It joined the National Register of Historic Places on March 21, 1997.
stops.fact: In 1897, the boxer Gentleman Jim Corbett trained here for a big fight against Bob Fitzsimmons.
stops.disputed: A famous theater man named David Belasco later published sensational stories about his time here. Historians treat his recollections as unreliable.

claims.t: The Piper's Opera House you can visit opened in 1885.
claims.why: The current building opened with a grand ball on March 6, 1885.

claims.t: The same building has stood here since 1863.
claims.why: The first two opera houses burned, in 1875 and 1883.

sources.t: National Park Service: National Register record for Piper's Opera House

spot.q: The 1937 photo shows the third Piper's Opera House. How many earlier opera houses burned before it opened in 1885?
spot.why: The first burned in the Great Fire of 1875 and the second on March 13, 1883. The third opened with a grand ball on March 6, 1885.

stops.name: Fourth Ward School
stops.teaser: A four-story school with a steep roof.
stops.map: 537 S C St, Virginia City, NV
stops.clue: Look for a big four-story school building on the south end of C Street. It has a steep roof and a lot of windows. It was built in 1876 for more than 1,000 students.
stops.safety: Stay on public sidewalks. The museum inside is optional and has its own hours. Do not climb fences or go into any old mine sites around town.
stops.field: Field notes pending: sidewalk slope and the viewing spot have not been checked on foot yet.

q.prompt: The marker in the museum's parking area says the school closed in what year?
q.hint: It closed during the Great Depression, after enrollment dropped below 200.
q.verify: HMDB marker at 537 S. C Street. Confirm on site.

then.label: The school in 1937
then.line: Built in 1876 for more than 1,000 students, with indoor plumbing and central heat. This photo was taken in March 1937.

link.t: Look for historic photos at the Library of Congress

now.head: Reopened
now.label: A school museum
now.line: The school reopened in 1986 as the Historic Fourth Ward School Museum. Photo from the Library of Congress, taken between 1980 and 2006.

story: The Fourth Ward School was built in 1876 in the Second Empire style, with a steep mansard roof and four stories. The architect was C. M. Bennett.
It was designed for more than 1,000 students. It had indoor plumbing, drinking fountains, gas lighting, and central heat. The last class graduated in 1936, and students moved to a new school.
The building sat closed and falling apart for years. In 1986 it reopened as the Historic Fourth Ward School Museum at 537 South C Street.
stops.fact: One building held primary school, grammar school, and high school under the same roof.
stops.disputed: Some pages call it the last wood-built school of its design in the United States. We could not find a source that backs that up.

claims.t: The Fourth Ward School graduated its last class in 1936.
claims.why: The school page gives 1936, when students moved to a new school.

claims.t: It is the last wood-built school of its design in the whole country.
claims.why: Some pages say so, but we found no source that backs it up.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Fourth Ward School (Virginia City, Nevada)

spot.q: The 1937 photo shows the Fourth Ward School, built in 1876. After the last class graduated in 1936, what became of the building?
options: It was torn down at once
It sat closed for years, then reopened as a museum in 1986
spot.why: It sat closed and falling apart for years, then reopened in 1986 as the Historic Fourth Ward School Museum.
